title: How Can a Mortal Be Righteous Before God?
summary: Job agrees that God is just in principle but asks how any human could win a case against him. He describes God's overwhelming power over mountains, sea, and stars, and concludes that even if he were innocent he could not answer such a judge. In his despair he says God destroys the blameless and the wicked alike, and he longs for a mediator who could stand between them.
story: Bildad has just told Job that God never perverts justice, so if Job is pure he need only seek God and be restored (chapter 8). Job's answer does not deny God's justice. Instead he raises a harder problem. If God is both the one accused and the judge of the case, and infinitely stronger than the man bringing it, how could the case ever be heard fairly? In this chapter the book's great legal metaphor comes fully into view. Job begins to imagine a trial with God, and that idea will grow through the coming chapters into his demand for a hearing (chapters 13 and 23) and his final signed oath of innocence (chapter 31). Verse 33, the longing for a mediator, starts a thread that runs into chapters 16 and 19.
historical:
Job's hymn to God's power in verses 5-10 draws on the sky and sea as ancient people knew them. Israel's neighbors watched the stars closely, and Babylonian astronomers kept careful records for calendars and omens. The constellations named in verse 9 were familiar night-sky markers across the region, used to track seasons for farming and travel. The Hebrew names are traditionally rendered the Bear, Orion, and the Pleiades, but the identifications rest partly on ancient translations and are not certain; the chambers or constellations of the south are harder still to pin down.

Rahab in verse 13 is not the woman of Jericho in Joshua 2, whose name is spelled differently in Hebrew. This Rahab is a poetic name for a monster of chaos, related to the sea imagery of chapter 7. Elsewhere in the Old Testament Rahab can also stand for Egypt (Psalm 87:4; Isaiah 30:7). Job's point is that even the powers other nations feared as cosmic rebels cower before God.
cultural:
The chapter is full of courtroom language. In Israel and its neighbors, disputes were settled at the city gate before elders, where each party presented his case, called witnesses, and waited for a verdict. The verb for contend in verse 3 (riv) is the word for bringing a lawsuit. Job imagines summoning God to court, answering his questions, and being declared righteous (verse 2 uses the legal sense of being in the right). But in any ancient court, a powerful man could intimidate a weaker one, and Job fears God will simply overwhelm him.

The mediator of verse 33 would have been a recognizable figure: an arbiter trusted by both parties, who could lay a hand on each, a gesture of authority over them both, and decide between them. Job's despair is that no such person exists, because no one stands above God. The images in verses 30-31 come from daily washing. Lye was an alkaline cleanser made from plant ash, and snow water was thought especially pure, yet Job says God would plunge him into the pit and make him filthy again.
literary: The chapter is built as a legal reflection that swings between hymn and accusation. Verses 2-4 set the question. Verses 5-13 are a hymn to God's power in creation, the kind of language found in the psalms of praise, but here it serves a dark point: such a God cannot be faced in court. Verses 14-24 apply this to Job's case with rising bitterness until he says that God destroys the innocent and the guilty alike. Verses 25-31 return to personal lament with images of speed (runner, papyrus boat, eagle). Verses 32-35 end with the wish for a mediator. The chapter opens with Job's question “how can a mortal be righteous before God?”, which picks up Eliphaz's question in 4:17 but turns it in a different direction: Eliphaz meant no one is morally pure; Job means no one can win a case against God.

outline.t: How can anyone win a case against God?
A hymn to God's overwhelming power
Even innocent, Job could not answer such a judge
Days that flee, and a cleansing that fails
No mediator between God and man

doctrines.note: Verses 4-10 describe God's wisdom and might: he moves mountains, commands the sun, stretches out the heavens, and makes the stars. Job does not doubt God's power; his anguish is that power without a visible justice looks like terror.
“If it is not He, then who is it?” (verse 24). Job refuses to explain his suffering by chance or by other powers. Everything is in God's hand, which makes his question sharper, not easier.
Job's cry for someone to stand between God and man names the need that the Bible answers with the idea of a mediator. Job himself does not see the answer; he only feels its absence.

words.note: Tsadaq, to be righteous or to be in the right. In a legal setting it means to be declared innocent in a case. Verse 2 asks how a mortal can be in the right before God, and verses 15 and 20 return to it. This is the same verb that lies behind later biblical language about justification.

Yakach, to decide, reprove, or argue a case. In verse 33 its participle names an arbiter or umpire, one who settles a dispute between two parties. Job's lament that there is no such figure is one of the book's most important moments.

Rahab, a name for a chaos monster in Hebrew poetry, related to a word meaning pride or storming. Its helpers bowing beneath God (verse 13) show that no cosmic power resists him. The word is different from the name of Rahab of Jericho.
Riv, to contend or bring a lawsuit. It sets the scene in verse 3: Job imagines a formal case with God and knows he could not answer one question in a thousand.

christ: Job's wish in verse 33, “Nor is there a mediator between us, to lay his hand upon us both,” is not a prophecy, but it names exactly what the New Testament says has been given. Paul writes that there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). Christians confess that Jesus is fully God and fully human, and so he can lay his hand on both parties in a way no other could. Hebrews presents him as the one who intercedes for his people (Hebrews 7:25). Job's question in verse 2 about how a mortal can be righteous before God becomes the central question of Paul's letter to the Romans, where the answer is a righteousness given by God through faith (Romans 3:21-26). Job longs for an arbiter; the gospel announces one.

hard.q: Job says God destroys the blameless and the wicked alike and mocks the innocent. Is the Bible saying that?
hard.a: In verses 22-24 Job says “He destroys both the blameless and the wicked,” that God mocks the despair of the innocent, and that he blindfolds the earth's judges. These are Job's words in the depth of his agony, not the narrator's verdict. The book lets him say them because they express how the world looks to someone in his position, and because the friends' tidy answers cannot be tested without them. The book does not endorse them as final. When God speaks in chapters 38 to 41, he challenges Job's accusations of injustice (40:8), and Job withdraws his words (42:6). Yet God also says Job spoke more rightly than his friends (42:7). Readers have taken this to mean that Job's honesty about what he could see was closer to the truth than the friends' false confidence, even though his conclusions went too far. The book allows both the protest and the correction.

questions: Job feels he could not win a hearing with God because God is so much greater. Have you ever felt that bringing your case to God was pointless? What helped, or what would?
Job longs for a mediator who could lay a hand on both God and him. What does it mean to you that Christians confess Jesus as that mediator?
Job praises God's power in verses 5-10 and yet finds no comfort in it. Why might God's power alone not be enough to comfort someone who is suffering?
